title: The King and the Dull Minister

keywords: the king and the dull minister
full_text:
In the court of Vijayanagara served a senior minister named Chandrashekar, whose only strategy for political survival was absolute, unquestioning flattery. Whatever King Krishnadevaraya said, Chandrashekar would nod vigorously and exclaim:
'Yes, Your Majesty! Absolutely, Maharaj! Your royal wisdom is incomparable!'

One morning, the King grew weary of this sycophancy.
Tenali Raman noticed the King’s irritation and whispered:
'Maharaj, allow me to demonstrate the danger of a minister who has lost the ability to say "No".'

Tenali stepped before the throne and said:
'Maharaj, I have conceived a brilliant municipal reform. To celebrate the coming festival, let us issue an imperial decree commanding that all citizens of Vijayanagara walk on their hands instead of their feet from dawn until noon!'

King Krishnadevaraya played along, nodding solemnly:
'A remarkable idea, Tenali! Minister Chandrashekar, what is your opinion of this royal reform?'

Chandrashekar, terrified of disagreeing with what seemed like a royal preference, bowed low:
'Yes, Your Majesty! A magnificent, divine decree! Walking on hands will strengthen the arms of our soldiers and elevate our subjects above common mortals!'

Tenali continued:
'And furthermore, Maharaj, to ensure public hygiene, let us decree that all cooks in the city must boil their rice in seawater and season it exclusively with powdered chalk!'

The King turned to the minister: 'Chandrashekar, what say you?'
Chandrashekar nodded enthusiastically:
'Yes, Maharaj! A masterstroke of culinary medicine! Chalk will whiten the teeth of the people, and seawater will preserve their health!'

Tenali then delivered the masterstroke:
'And finally, Maharaj, since Minister Chandrashekar agrees so passionately with every single measure, let us decree that he shall be the first to demonstrate them!
Let him walk on his hands three times around the palace outer moat, while eating a bowl of rice boiled in seawater and seasoned with chalk!'

Chandrashekar’s eyes bulged in horror!
He fell prostrate upon the carpet, sweating, waving his hands frantically:
'No, no, no! Mercy, Your Majesty! I cannot walk on my hands! Seawater and chalk will poison my stomach!'

The King and the entire court burst into thunderous laughter!
King Krishnadevaraya looked down sternly at the trembling flatterer:
'Chandrashekar, thou didst find thy "No" only when thine own stomach was in peril!
A ruler who is surrounded by men who say "Yes" to every folly is a blind man walking toward a precipice. The state needs ministers with the courage to say "No" when an idea is harmful to the people.'

Chandrashekar was demoted, while Tenali showed that honest disagreement in council is the truest pillar of good governance.
moral: Flattery that agrees blindly with every word of power is dangerous to an empire; true loyalty exercises independent judgment.
